paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.29:1 Rule 4.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.29. 1. Specific Requirements Further, to effect the application of the rule, specific notice that the offer to settle is made pursuant to R. 170 must be given if the plaintiff seeks to limit the court's general discretion to award costs by the provisions of R. 174(2). That rule requires the court to award double costs, unless a “special reason” permits the court to order otherwise when the plaintiff recovers a sum equal to or greater than the amount of the terms of his offer of settlement made pursuant to R. 170 … I read R. 174(2) to mean the plaintiff must make and specify that his offer of settlement is made pursuant to the provisions of R. 170 to make it applicable. That makes eminent good sense. Not every offer of settlement made by a plaintiff is an offer under RR. 170 and 174. Often a plaintiff will make an offer of settlement in which he does not threaten double costs for purposes of negotiating a settlement. The applicant's contention that it is not necessary to specify the offer is made pursuant to R. 170 would make R. 170 applicable to all settlement proposals unless otherwise specified. That, to me, is untenable. Practical common sense dictates otherwise. Alberta (Treasury Branches) v. Floral Holdings Ltd. (1990), 73 Alta. L.R. (2d) 283 (Q.B.), at 285-86, per Mason J. Problems with the wording of an offer do not necessarily invalidate it. Counsel for the plaintiff submits that the plaintiff's offer should not be treated as an offer pursuant to R. 170 because an offer made pursuant to that Rule should call for payment into court, and not to the plaintiff. He submits the offer should be treated as an offer of settlement subject to common law and that it could be withdrawn at any time before it was accepted. In my opinion there is no merit in that argument. The plaintiff clearly intended to make an offer pursuant to R. 170 and the problems with the wording of the offer are really only matters of form and not substance. Except for the mistake made in the amount of the plaintiff's claim it can be safely assumed the plaintiff would be satisfied if it received the money one way or another. 421990 Alberta Ltd. v. Royal Trust Corp. of Canada (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 404 (Master), at 405-406, per Master Quinn. The comments of the learned Master should be taken to mean no more than if the facts taken as a whole would lead to the conclusion that the offer was made pursuant to the rule, then defects in the form of the offer will not rebut that conclusion. 2. The Effect of Set-Off In Carroll v. Atco Electric Ltd., 2017 ABQB 641, 2017 CarswellAlta 2017, [2018] 3 W.W.R. 805, the Plaintiff (Carroll) had been granted judgment in the amount of $72,000 for “foregone bonuses arising from a without cause dismissal” by the Defendant. However it was also found that “the actual salary paid during the notice period, combined with a ‘with prejudice’ payment subsequently made by ATCO Electric plus Carroll's mitigation income, exceeded the amount payable for 24 months' notice by some $165,208.” The Defendant “was entitled to equitably set-off the excess against the judgment and was relieved of any further liability.” At the end of the day, Carroll had “failed at trial to best any of four offers made by ATCO Electric along the way.” The Defendant sought double costs from the time of the second offer it made. Justice Mah held that the facts did not support an award of double costs. His Lordship said: 8 The assertion of entitlement to double costs from the second offer arises from the fact that second offer, made on October 5, 2012, was coupled with a cash “with prejudice” payment of $150,000 which created the bulk of the excess. It is argued that the effect of ATCO Electric becoming entitled to set-off the excess against the judgment per 2017 ABQB 426 nullified the Carroll's judgment, with the net result that Carroll's action was “dismissed” in its entirety for the purposes of Rule 4.29(3)(b). 9 Carroll's counsel counters that his claim against ATCO Electric was not and has never been dismissed. He achieved a judgment of $72,000. He has only been prevented from collecting it because of the set-off ruling. 10 I agree with Carroll's counsel here. It is clear from para 125 of 2017 ABQB 267 that I rendered judgment in Carroll's favour. I did not dismiss the claim for the 2010 and 2011 bonuses but rather upheld it. In the subsequent decision I ruled that, in equity, ATCO Electric should not be required to pay further. That does not detract from the fact that Carroll obtained the judgment in the first place. 11 Accordingly, I find that ATCO Electric is not entitled to double costs from the date of the second offer … 3. Demand for Apology in Defamation Actions In Vaquero Energy Ltd. v. Weir, 2004 ABQB 166, 2004 CarswellAlta 389, 352 A.R. 398, 54 Alta. L.R. (4th) 254, the plaintiff successfully sued the defendant for defamation. The plaintiff had served the defendant with a Rule 170 offer of settlement which required the defendant to pay $25,000 and to acknowledge responsibility for the defamatory remarks. The issue was whether the demand for an acknowledgment of responsibility for the defamatory remarks fit within Rule 170. Kent J. held that it did. At p. 400, her Ladyship said: The defendant in this case says that because the court has no ability to order an apology, the plaintiff cannot demand it. I disagree. In a defamation action, a finding that what was said or printed was defamatory is often as important as the amount of a money judgment. That finding is equivalent to a pre-trial apology. A pre-judgment apology would serve the purpose of Rule 170, namely to encourage settlement. Accordingly, an offer of judgment in a defamation action that includes a demand for an apology or acknowledgment falls within the scope of Rule 170. 4. When the Rule Results in Over Indemnification in Costs In Shillingford v. Dalbridge Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 28, 2000 CarswellAlta 48, 268 A.R. 324, 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 361, Perras, J. held that costs calculated pursuant to Rule 174 should be awarded even if they result in a party receiving an over indemnification for his or her actual legal costs. At p. 369, His Lordship said: It is my view, considering the above, that party/party costs where there has been a formal offer of settlement under the Rules of Court should be taxed based on the tariff amounts as set under Schedule C and as outlined in Rule 174, notwithstanding that [an] over indemnification may occur. This would promote settlement by punishing those who refuse reasonable offers. Furthermore, it would provide an even playing field irrespective of the actual cost of the lawyer, or the fact that a party is represented through legal aid or self represented. … In Jama v. Bobolo, 2002 ABQB 216, 2002 CarswellAlta 435, 311 A.R. 362, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 186, Clark J., at p. 191, said that: “Despite the possibility that over-indemnification may occur, it may indeed be appropriate to award double costs.” His Lordship implied that if the application of the provisions of Rule 174(2) would normally result in an award of double costs, the onus to show why that award should not exceed indemnification would fall on the party paying the costs. He said, at pp. 191-192: Thus, the rule appears to be that if a party wants to continue to advance its claim, following an offer of settlement, it does so at its peril. … As there are no special reasons that would dictate in favour of restricting costs to indemnification in the present case, double costs are appropriate. 5. Reason for R. 4.29 People sometimes ask why a plaintiff who equals or beats her own offer gets higher costs. There are two reasons. First, unless a plaintiff's costs are going to be increased, there is no incentive whatever for the defendant to pay any attention to any plaintiff's offer to settle. A plaintiff who recovers anything significant at trial will get single costs even without any offer. Second, Rule 174 treats the plaintiff and the defendant similarily. A defendant who equals or beats his own offer in effect gets double costs: (a) the defendant is awarded costs in his favour. And (b) the plaintiff gets no costs despite her substantial recovery, though normally she would get full single costs. A plaintiff who had neither made nor received any offer almost invariably gets full party-party costs of the suit, even if her pleadings claimed too much. A party who sued for exactly what she is entitled and did not inflate her claim should not be penalized. Jones v. Trans America Life Insurance Co. of Canada (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.), at 5, per curiam. 6. Purpose of R. 4.29(4)(a) In 864503 Alberta Inc. v. Genco Place Properties Ltd., 2019 ABCA 248, 2019 CarswellAlta 1161, the Court said: … The purpose of rule 4.29(4)(a) is to avoid the doubling of indemnity or lump sum costs following a formal offer. It does not have the effect of rendering a formal offer following an award of lump sum costs to be of no effect in respect of subsequent costs. 7. When Over-indemnification may constitute a “special circumstance” under R. 4.29(4)(e) In Mostafa Altalibi Professional Corporation v. Lorne S. Kamelchuk Professional Corporation, 2022 ABCA 364, 2022 CarswellAlta 3300, the Court discussed when over-indemnification might constitute a “special circumstance”: [34] In some circumstances, the possibility of significant over-indemnification may constitute a special circumstance to not award double costs. For example, where solicitor and own client costs are awarded, this Court has stated that the doubling of such costs may constitute a special circumstance under r 4.29(4)(e): Boje v Boje (Estate of), 2005 ABCA 73 at para 39. However, this Court also stated that the double costs regime may in some circumstances even apply to awards of solicitor and own client costs: Boje at para 39. [35] The purpose of the double costs regime in the Alberta Rules of Court is to encourage settlement and to ensure that a party which “gambles and loses” on an appeal accepts greater consequences for doing so: H2S at para 18. [36] In this case, no evidence has been provided that a double costs award would result in over-indemnification. Absent such evidence, there is no basis to depart from the standard application of the double costs regime in the Alberta Rules of Court. The respondents are seeking party-party costs, not solicitor and own client costs. Therefore, the considerations identified in Boje do not apply here. Double costs awards will be greater than standard costs awards by their very nature. The mere possibility of over-indemnification is not a special circumstance within the meaning of r 4.29(4)(e). 8. Compare Offer to Judgment One should compare the offer to the judgment, but an issue arises concerning whether or not to include costs in the comparison. In McAteer v. Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 2003 CarswellAlta 654, 340 A.R. 1, 21 Alta. L.R. (4th) 115, Rooke J. considered the question of determining whether an offer exceeded the judgment awarded. At pp. 135-137, his Lordship said: There are two lines of authority that guide this comparison. One method of calculating the value of an offer in relation to the judgment is discussed in Steve's Contracting Ltd. v. Williams et al. (1997), 214 A.R. 318 (Q.B.) (Andrekson, J.). The court in that case acknowledged that there is very little Alberta case law that discusses this issue. Accordingly, Andrekson, J., began his analysis with a review of the rule in Ontario that emanated from the decision in Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. v. Cassina (1992), 15 C.P.C. (3d) 264 (Ont. Gen Div.—Rosenburg, J.). At p. 266 of that decision, the court found that: …the proper test is to look at the offer compared to the amount recovered plus interest and costs up to the date of the offer. The court in Steve's Contracting looked at a number of decisions of the Alberta Court of Appeal in order to assess whether the same rule was applicable in Alberta. It noted that in Ness v. Leveridge (1995), 174 A.R. 283, 102 W.A.C. 283, 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 407 at p. 411 (Alta. L.R.), the Court of Appeal stated, at para. 13 “The two ‘judgments’ must refer to amounts calculated in the same manner.” Cognizant of this requirement, the court, thus, compared the offer at para. 19 of Steve's: The plaintiff's offer … plus prejudgment interest to and including the date of the service of the offer, plus taxable party/party costs (including reasonable disbursements) for steps taken in all three actions up to and including the date of service of the offer is equal to or greater than the judgment amount … plus prejudgment interest to and including the date of service of the offer, plus taxable party/party costs (including reasonable disbursements) for steps taken in all 3 actions up to and including the date of service of the offer. This formula has also been adopted by this court in Hillside Investments Ltd. v. Boychuk, [2002] A.J. No. 33, [2002] A.R. Uned. 231 (Q.B.—Marshall, J.) and Greep v. Josephson et al. (2001), 285 A.R. 326 (Q.B.) (Romaine, J.). [59] The other line of authority suggests that costs should not be considered when comparing an offer to the judgment amount. The Alberta Court of Appeal dealt with this issue in Pugsley v. Wong et al., [2001] A.J. No. 1570, [2001] A.R. Uned. 293. At para. 4 the court, without citing any authority, in a very brief Memorandum of Judgment discussed the formula to be used in effecting a comparison: The reported cases on how to calculate whether the plaintiff has bettered an unaccepted offer usually compare damages and interest, not costs. The reason for both things doubtless is rule 169(2), which allows a plaintiff, who accepts the defendant's offer, at once to tax her costs to that point. Therefore, we conclude that we should not look at costs, and that the plaintiff plainly did not better the offer. However, this comment in Pugsley appears to be obiter dicta. Moreover, that case involved a situation where including the costs in the comparison would not have effected the result. This fact was acknowledged by the court, at para. 6, where it stated “In case we are wrong, it probably would make very little difference here.” Additionally, the case deals with an offer by the defendant under the Rules which, as noted, allows the plaintiff to tax costs. This is distinguishable from the case here, where the Offer was a Calderbank offer extended by the plaintiff which specifically included costs in its terms. Finally, there is no suggestion that the Court of Appeal considered or even less so, intended, to reverse Ness. In the result, I do not believe that I am bound by the obiter statement in Pugsley. Rather, I find that the Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ness and cases to that effect are a better statement of the law in the context of the case at bar. Examined from a principled point of view, I am of the view that the best approach is not to adopt a strict formula that will be used in all cases regardless of the terms of the offer. There may be situations in which the comparison of costs is of little assistance. One example would appear to be Pugsley. In order to make a correct comparison, the total value of the offer must be considered in relation to the total value of the judgment as at the date of the offer. In other words, it is inappropriate to exclude significant variables that may differ considerably. In this case the judgment included an award of solicitor/client costs to Mason from the commencement of the Mason and Originating Notice Actions. This amount differs considerably from the party/party costs that were included in the Offer. It is therefore imperative that costs be included in the comparison in the present case. In Alberta Wheat Pool v. Fieldberg, 2001 ABQB 669, 2001 CarswellAlta 1007, 296 A.R. 161, the plaintiff offered to settle its claim by discontinuing its action if the defendant discontinued its three counterclaims, all without costs. The defendant rejected the offer, and at trial, the plaintiff was awarded judgment in the amount of $41,770, two of the counterclaims were dismissed, and the third counterclaim resulted in the defendant (plaintiff by counterclaim) being awarded judgment in the amount of $611.36. In deciding that the plaintiff was entitled to double costs because it had recovered judgment in excess of its offer, Lee J., at p. 166, said: …[T]he Offer that was made by Alberta Wheat Pool to settle this matter has a clear intent which was that both parties would walk away from their respective actions without either party receiving any costs. My judgment was a substantive judgment of $41,770.00 in favour of the Plaintiff Alberta Wheat Pool, and essentially a nominal judgment of $611.36 on one of Mr. Fieldberg's three Counterclaims, the other two Counterclaims being dismissed in their entirety. Surely the Court should look at the overall intention of the Offer, and determine if based on that overall intention the Plaintiff was successful enough to earn double costs as part of a broad and liberal interpretation of Rule 174(2). If Mr. Fieldberg had accepted the Alberta Wheat Pool's Offer, he would have walked away owing nothing to the Alberta Wheat Pool. It is clear that the Plaintiff has beaten its Offer in that Mr. Fieldberg now owes them a net judgment of slightly over $41,000.00. Given that the intention of the settlement provisions of the Alberta Rules of Court are to reduce the costs of litigation and encourage the resolution of lawsuits early, it is arguable that the Court should award double costs to the Plaintiff on both the claim and the Counterclaim for all steps taken after July 30, 1998. However, given the possible confusion here arising out of the nature of the Offer of Settlement, I will award only double costs to the Plaintiff in its action against Mr. Fieldberg in which it was clearly successful. In Whitford v. Agrium Inc., 2007 ABCA 109, 2007 CarswellAlta 445, the plaintiff made a formal offer to the defendant which was inclusive of costs and interest. The offer was not accepted, and a judgment was awarded after trial. The Court held that in determining whether the judgment obtained was more favourable to the plaintiff than the offer made, one must look at the costs and interest at the time of the offer, not at the time of judgment. Slatter, J.A. said: 2 The plaintiff commenced a wrongful dismissal action against the defendant, and on September 9th, 2004 made a formal offer of $94,000.00, inclusive of costs and interest. At trial in March of 2006 the plaintiff was awarded $81,834.78. If costs and interest accrued to the date of the offer were added to the damage award, the judgment was less favourable than the offer. However, if costs and interest accrued to the date of the judgment were added to the damage award, then the eventual result was more favourable than the offer. The trial judge compared the offer to the judgment as if costs and interest to the date of judgment were included, and awarded double costs. The question on this appeal is therefore how one calculates the amount of a judgment for the purpose of comparing it to an offer. 3 As a general rule, for the purposes of calculating costs, a judgment should be valued as if it included interest and costs up to the date of the offer only, not up to the date of trial. The plaintiff's offer can only be “more favourable than” the judgment if the defendant would, on the date of offer, have been better off to accept the offer than suffer the eventual judgment. It is inconsistent with the objectives of the Rules on formal offers to say that a plaintiff or a defendant can, by running up costs between the date of the offer and the trial, achieve a more favourable result. When the offer is inclusive of costs, the proper approach is to add costs (including disbursements) and interest to the date of the offer, as set out in Steve's Contracting Ltd. v. Williams (1997), 214 A.R. 318, Hillside Investments Ltd. v. Boychuk, [2002] A.J. No. 33, 2002 ABQB 26 at para. 6; McAteer v. Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 21 Alta. L.R. (4th) 116, at para. 60; and Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. v. Cassina (1992), 15 C.P.C. (3d) 264 (Ont. Gen. Div.). How the offeror came up with the amount of a lump sum offer, and what sub-components of the lump sum the offeror subjectively thought the offer contained, are not relevant to the assessment of whether the offer is “more favourable”. In the end, the comparison is between the total amount of the offer, on the one hand, and on the other, the principal amount recovered on all heads of damage plus pre-judgment interest and costs (including disbursements) to the date of the offer. 4 The purpose of the rules is to encourage early reasonable settlements, thereby avoiding the costs and delay inherent in litigation. To interpret the rules so as to allow costs and interest to be calculated right up to the date of judgment runs counter to those objectives because: a) it creates an incentive for the offeror to run up costs after the offer is made. b) at the early stages of litigation, where the required interlocutory steps and length of trial are uncertain and unpredictable, it would be difficult for the offeror to calculate, and the offeree to evaluate, an offer. This is contrary to the policy of encouraging early settlement. c) it requires the offeree to pay a settlement premium or penalty equal to the costs of a trial, where the purpose of the rule is to avoid that trial and those very costs. d) a different rule would apply to offers inclusive of costs, compared to offers made “plus costs to be taxed”. It is not suggested that a “plus costs” offer is properly compared to a judgment plus costs to the date of trial. … 7 In 2003, Rule 174(1)(b) relating to defendants offers was changed so that it also read “more favourable than”. The wording “more favourable than” calls for a functional comparison of the judgment with the offer. 8 In this case the plaintiff's offer was clearly not more favourable than the judgment achieved. One of the purposes of offers is to end litigation, thereby stopping the accrual of costs by both parties. The offer by the plaintiff to accept $94,000 turned out to be more than what the defendant would have been liable to pay as of the date of the offer, and the defendant was entitled to reject it. The plaintiff's offer turned out to be too high, and it cannot become “more favourable” simply because the plaintiff thereafter incurred more costs that a lower offer might well have avoided: Steve's Contracting at para. 9; Jones v. Trans America Life Insurance Co. of Canada (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.). 9. Being Close Is Not Enough The Appellant urges, as one of the reasons why he should be awarded costs of the appeal, that the amount he recovered is very close to the amount paid in, and that the damages were low. Therefore, he says, the Court should exercise a discretion not to apply the rule. In my opinion, however, those factors, of themselves, would not entitle the Appellant to escape the effects of rule 174. Rahmath v. Louisiana Land & Exploration Co. (1989), 104 A.R. 391 at 392 (C.A.). The Court of Appeal also stated: … the present R. 174 is designed to remove flexibility, absent truly “special reason”. It appears to us that a near miss, or a payment into court only six days before trial, does not present such “special reason”. Brown Estate v. Young (1990), 73 Alta. L.R. (2d) 66 at 68 (C.A.). In Patterson v. Hryciuk, 2005 ABQB 136, 2005 CarswellAlta 309, 45 Alta. L.R. (4th) 240, a plaintiff was granted judgment for $48,967.59 in a medical malpractice action. She then sought costs “in excess of those prescribed under Column 2 of Schedule C”, claiming that “the Defendant refused to accept a Formal Offer to Settle served on him prior to trial which was ‘close enough’ to the judgment.” The judgment awarded was $1,032.41 less than the offer made by the Plaintiff. Macklin J. declined to grant increased costs. His Lordship said, at pp. 248-249: Rule 601(1) of the Alberta Rules sets out the factors which the court may consider when exercising its discretion in awarding costs. They include the result in a proceeding and a number of other factors, none of which specifically include offers made by the parties to settle the matter prior to trial. They do specify that the court may “consider any other matter relevant to the question of costs”. There is also nothing in the compromise rules (Part 12, Rules 165 to 174) which would suggest that the court has discretion to take into account offers that do not meet the requirements set out therein for an award of additional costs. They only speak in terms of offers that meet or beat the trial result. Without an express provision allowing the court to consider inadequate but “close” offers, I do not feel it proper to consider them in determining the appropriate level of costs. Rule 174 provides specific consequences where the Defendant refuses an offer and the judgment at trial is greater than the amount of the offer. It does not allow consideration of the offer if it was close to or within a certain percentage of the award. Where the rules are specific as to their effect, it is not appropriate to rely on a general provision to confer a benefit otherwise not earned. Without any specific allowance for it, the court would be required in each case to assess the offer in light of the final result and demarcate a line over or under which the offer should be considered close enough to warrant cost consequences. In terms of procedure, it is my view that unless there is a specific rule allowing a court to consider it, it is inappropriate for one party to hold up a compromise offer made by the other party and argue that the offeror should be somehow punished in costs for its inadequate offer. Only offers that meet the requirements of the compromise rules, thereby allowing the court to consider them in its award of costs, should be brought to the attention of the court after judgment. Unless and until there is a rule allowing the court to consider all offers made in writing (as in the other jurisdictions referred to above), those offers should be considered as having been made without prejudice and privileged for all purposes. That is, they are irrelevant to the costs determination and should remain confidential as between the parties. Further, and in any event, while the Defendant's offer may be seen as an unreasonable position given the outcome at trial, it is also a position that can easily be rationalized by a belief that there was no liability on the part of the defendant. This is not a situation where the only issue was quantum and the defendant refused to consider payment of any amount notwithstanding its liability. A defendant is entitled to defend an action and is entitled to maintain a defence on both liability and quantum. Unless he refuses an offer that satisfies the requirements of the compromise rules and there is no other rule specifically allowing the court to consider the offer, the defendant should not be penalized by any increased award of costs. In short, the Plaintiff is not entitled to any increase in its costs for serving an offer close to the judgment amount. In Alberta, there is no single point for a missed field goal. 10. Onus Lies on Party Relying on the Rule In Alberta, the law as to who has the onus under Rule 174 to prove that a judgement obtained after trial was equal to or greater than his offer under Rule 170 is correctly set out in Stevenson & Côté's Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2000 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1999). At page 134 the authors state: “The party relaying [sic] on the Rule has the onus of proving that he did better at trial than the offer”. Madge v. Meyer (2000), 77 Alta. L.R. (3d) 391 (Q.B.) at 397, per Brooker, J. 11. Offer Must Satisfy High Degree of Certainty In Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R. 307, 9 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, the plaintiff sought double costs under Rule 174(2) on the grounds that the plaintiff obtained at trial a judgment in excess of the offer the plaintiff had made to settle the action. Fraser, J. in refusing the application noted that “[i]n the offer in question, the plaintiffs purported to reserve leave to seek advice and rulings from a Court of Queen's Bench Justice ‘as they in their sole unfettered discretion may determine’ on any and all issues concerning costs” (p. 314). Fraser J. said, at p. 314: The defendants also cite Laframboise v. Billett (1991), 81 Alta. L.R. (2d) 285 (Q.B.); rev'd on other grounds (1992), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 394 (C.A.), in which MacLean, J. (as he then was), stated (at para. 3): The consequences of the Rules as to costs contained in Part 12 of the Rules of Court are punitive, and therefore demand a very high degree of certainty and exactness. The defendant's offer of settlement does not satisfy that high degree of certainty and exactness, and he is therefore not entitled to the benefit of those Rules and his application in that regard is dismissed. Laframboise has been cited with approval in subsequent decisions, including Madge v. Meyer et al. (2000), 259 A.R. 351, 81 Alta. L.R. (2d) 285 (Q.B.), at para. 10 [Alta. L.R.], and Garand v. Mutual of Omaha Insurance Co. et al. (2001), 297 A.R. 286, ¶ 20 (Q.B.). With respect, I adopt the principle underlying Laframboise, and find that service of the May 17 offer to settle did not, in the circumstances, require the doubling of fees. 12. Results of Mini-trial Are Irrelevant In Purich v. Purich (1999), 248 A.R. 145 (Q.B.), the defendant in a support and matrimonial property action alleged that the plaintiff had not done as well at trial as had been earlier offered to her. In support of that submission, the defendant referred to discussions which occurred in the mini-trial. Veit J. held that mini-trials should not be considered when determining the issue of costs. At pp. 147-49: The outcome of a mini-trial should not, without more, be taken into account in determining what costs should be paid at the conclusion of a trial. . . . . . Settlement negotiations are, generally, privileged. The privilege supports the under lying policy that fair settlements are a worthwhile objective and that parties should feel free to make concessions for the purposes of settlement which should not come back to haunt them if no settlement is, in fact, reached. The Rules create a statutory interference with the privilege in order to give punch to certain, defined, types of offers of settlement. The common law establishes that a party can put the party opposite on notice that if an offer of settlement is not accepted, that party intends to ask for costs. Without such glosses of the privilege, no reference at all could be made to settlement negotiations at the costs hearing because those negotiations are privileged. A mini-trial is just another form of settlement negotiations. Without some legislated term or some understanding between the parties that the mini-trial will be referred to at the costs hearing, it is improper for the court to be advised of the results of a mini-trial. 13. Costs' Effect on Judgment Not a “Special Reason” In a defendant's application for double costs, the successful plaintiff submitted that these ought not to be awarded because this would effectively take from her the judgment granted to her at trial. The court held that such a submission was irrelevant. In the absence of exceptional circumstances, a court should not hesitate to award appropriate costs even if the results of the costs award would be to deprive a litigant of the financial benefit of the substantive litigation. In this case, Ms. Bates claims that if the court were to award costs to Mr. Purich on the basis he proposes, the costs award would be so high that it would effectively deprive Ms. Bates of the benefit of her judgment. Ms. Bates' argument is irrelevant. The potential award of costs is meant to promote reasonable settlements. If, indeed, there were a case where the costs were so high as to be equivalent to, or even higher than, the substantive amount in question, there should be an even greater impetus to be reasonable. The court must make a costs determination on the basis of the principles that apply to such determinations. The fact that a proper costs determination will deprive a litigant of the fruits of the litigation only proves that in that particular case, the litigation was pointless; for policy reasons, the unreasonable litigant should not profit in the slightest from unnecessary litigation. Purich v. Purich (1999), 248 A.R. 145 (Q.B.), at 149, per Veit J. See also, “Special Reasons”, infra, under this rule. 14. When Defendant Makes Offer Not Beaten by Plaintiff at Trial In Lawler v. Ron's Coach & Bus Repairs Inc. (1998), 68 Alta. L.R. (3d) 107 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Burrows said, at p. 109: It has been observed in many cases that though a Plaintiff who beats an offer of judgment made by the Plaintiff under Rule 170 gets double costs, a Defendant who beats an offer of judgment made by the Defendant under Rule 169, gets only single costs. If the Defendant beats the offer but is still found liable, the effect is that he or she avoids payment of the Plaintiff's costs and receives costs from the time of the offer. In such a situation the effect is equivalent to a doubling of costs. In Mitran v. Guarantee RV Centre Inc. (1999), 72 Alta. L.R. (3d) 54 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone commented on R. 174(1.1) (current R. 4.29(3)(b) which permits the defendant to obtain double costs if the defendant is successful in having the plaintiff's claim dismissed in its entirety. At pp. 58-59, Her Ladyship said: In 1998, amendments were made to the Rules of Court to allow a defendant to collect double costs where an offer is made, the plaintiff fails to accept it, and the claim against the defendant is dismissed at trial. . . . . . The wording of the Rules in conjunction with s. 327(2) of the Insurance Act make it clear that the judgment offered pursuant to R. 169 and the judgment potentially recoverable at trial are to be calculated in the same manner. Section B benefits received by a claimant in the position of the Respondent must be credited against his damages in calculating the amount of any judgment recovered at trial. It follows that the amount of the judgment tendered in an Offer of Judgment must be exclusive of Section B benefits. A failure to state that in the Offer cannot create an ambiguity. A plaintiff who receives an Offer of Judgment may accept it and, pursuant to R. 169(2), file the Offer and Acceptance in Court and then “apply to the court for judgment in accordance with the offer …” The “judgment” for which the offeree may apply on acceptance is one “in accordance with the offer”, that is, in the amount set out in the Offer of Judgment made pursuant to R. 169(1). The cost sanction provided by R. 174(1) arises where the “judgment” recovered at trial does not exceed the “judgment”offered in the Offer of Judgment. The two “judgments” must refer to amounts calculated in the same manner. Had the Respondent accepted the Offer, he would have been entitled to file it and an acceptance and apply to the Court for judgment in the sum of $40,000, plus judgment interest and taxable costs. Rule 169 contemplates a judgment in the amount offered without any adjustments. At the same time, s. 327(2) of the Insurance Act makes it abundantly clear that a claimant in the position of the Respondent is not entitled to a judgment which includes amounts received by him from his own insurer by way of Section B benefits. A defendant who makes an unqualified Offer of Judgment intending to deduct Section B benefits if it is accepted runs the risk that the Offer will be accepted and judgment thereafter entered, “in accordance with the Offer”, for an amount which includes them. Section B benefits are not analogous to pre-judgment interest. The former are, by definition, excluded from forming part of the judgment, while the latter, like costs, may or may not, depending on the circumstances and the discretion of the trial judge. The recovery of pre-judgment interest and costs are not certainties and it is therefore imperative that an Offer of Judgment states clearly whether or not it includes them. Amounts received as Section B benefits cannot be recovered in any circumstances and the “judgment” offered in an Offer of Judgment is net of those amounts. In our view, it is not necessary to refer to Section B benefits in an Offer of Judgment. The failure to do so does not render the Offer ambiguous and constitute a “special reason” for not imposing the cost sanction provided by R. 174(1). Where a settlement offer does not contain an element of compromise, the court may nevertheless consider it to have been reasonable in the circumstances and exercise its discretion to award enhanced costs. An offer of settlement that does not realistically reflect the relative merit of the parties' positions at the time it is made is not a genuine offer. The assessment of an offer's genuineness is not confined to a consideration of whether it was made honestly and in good faith. The fact it contains an element of compromise, although necessary and relevant, may not be determinative. The genuineness of an offer must be assessed as at the time it was served and remained open and its character cannot be decided by simply comparing it to the result of the trial or appeal. None of these factors, or any other single factor, is necessarily conclusive. An assessment of whether an offer was or was not genuine requires an examination of all of the surrounding circumstances, subjective and objective, existing at the time the offer was served and remained open, as well as the outcome of the trial or appeal. Were the law otherwise, a plaintiff would feel entitled to advance a weak cause of action secure in the expectation that they would have to be bought off by some form of material cash payment. As the government put it, a plaintiff should not proceed as if they are entitled to benefit from the litigation. 22 The plaintiff suggests that, if she had been offered somewhat more cash, say $5,000.00, that she might have settled. She argues that case law, including Allen, suggests that a genuine offer is one for which there is a “reasonable expectation that it will be accepted”, and that “the addition of an offer to forego costs … does not include an element of compromise”. These comments by our Court of Appeal must be assessed in the context in which they were made; in particular, the Allen comments focus on situations where a plaintiff makes an offer to settle for the full amount of, or even more than (see the reference to Labbee at paras. 11 and 15), the amount of its claim. It is obvious that a plaintiff who states that they will settle for having their claim paid in full is not making a genuine offer whereas a defendant who is offering to take the benefit of a judgment while giving up its costs is actually giving up something. 23 In this case, the Alberta Government's offers were clearly in excess of the court's judgment: the court found that Ms. Snihur did not have a valid cause of action against the government and denied her claim in its entirety. Therefore, if the government's offers were valid offers pursuant to the Rules, Alberta is entitled to a rebuttable presumption in favour of double costs: Partec Lavalin Inc. [2002 ABCA 114] at para. 7.
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 4 (Part 3)

sentences.text: Commentary § 4.29:1 Rule 4.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Specific Requirements Further, to effect the application of the rule, specific notice that the offer to settle is made pursuant to R.
170 must be given if the plaintiff seeks to limit the court's general discretion to award costs by the provisions of R.

That rule requires the court to award double costs, unless a “special reason” permits the court to order otherwise when the plaintiff recovers a sum equal to or greater than the amount of the terms of his offer of settlement made pursuant to R.
170 … I read R.
174(2) to mean the plaintiff must make and specify that his offer of settlement is made pursuant to the provisions of R.
170 to make it applicable.
That makes eminent good sense.
Not every offer of settlement made by a plaintiff is an offer under RR.
Often a plaintiff will make an offer of settlement in which he does not threaten double costs for purposes of negotiating a settlement.
The applicant's contention that it is not necessary to specify the offer is made pursuant to R.
170 would make R.
170 applicable to all settlement proposals unless otherwise specified.
That, to me, is untenable.
Practical common sense dictates otherwise.
Alberta (Treasury Branches) v.
Floral Holdings Ltd.
L.R.
(2d) 283 (Q.B.), at 285-86, per Mason J.
Problems with the wording of an offer do not necessarily invalidate it.
Counsel for the plaintiff submits that the plaintiff's offer should not be treated as an offer pursuant to R.
170 because an offer made pursuant to that Rule should call for payment into court, and not to the plaintiff.
He submits the offer should be treated as an offer of settlement subject to common law and that it could be withdrawn at any time before it was accepted.
In my opinion there is no merit in that argument.
The plaintiff clearly intended to make an offer pursuant to R.
170 and the problems with the wording of the offer are really only matters of form and not substance.
Except for the mistake made in the amount of the plaintiff's claim it can be safely assumed the plaintiff would be satisfied if it received the money one way or another.
421990 Alberta Ltd. v.
Royal Trust Corp. of Canada (1995), 30 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 404 (Master), at 405-406, per Master Quinn.

The comments of the learned Master should be taken to mean no more than if the facts taken as a whole would lead to the conclusion that the offer was made pursuant to the rule, then defects in the form of the offer will not rebut that conclusion.
The Effect of Set-Off In Carroll v.
Atco Electric Ltd., 2017 ABQB 641, 2017 CarswellAlta 2017, [2018] 3 W.W.R.
805, the Plaintiff (Carroll) had been granted judgment in the amount of $72,000 for “foregone bonuses arising from a without cause dismissal” by the Defendant.

However it was also found that “the actual salary paid during the notice period, combined with a ‘with prejudice’ payment subsequently made by ATCO Electric plus Carroll's mitigation income, exceeded the amount payable for 24 months' notice by some $165,208.” The Defendant “was entitled to equitably set-off the excess against the judgment and was relieved of any further liability.” At the end of the day, Carroll had “failed at trial to best any of four offers made by ATCO Electric along the way.” The Defendant sought double costs from the time of the second offer it made.
Justice Mah held that the facts did not support an award of double costs.

His Lordship said: 8 The assertion of entitlement to double costs from the second offer arises from the fact that second offer, made on October 5, 2012, was coupled with a cash “with prejudice” payment of $150,000 which created the bulk of the excess.

It is argued that the effect of ATCO Electric becoming entitled to set-off the excess against the judgment per 2017 ABQB 426 nullified the Carroll's judgment, with the net result that Carroll's action was “dismissed” in its entirety for the purposes of Rule 4.29(3)(b).
9 Carroll's counsel counters that his claim against ATCO Electric was not and has never been dismissed.
He achieved a judgment of $72,000.
He has only been prevented from collecting it because of the set-off ruling.
10 I agree with Carroll's counsel here.
It is clear from para 125 of 2017 ABQB 267 that I rendered judgment in Carroll's favour.
I did not dismiss the claim for the 2010 and 2011 bonuses but rather upheld it.
In the subsequent decision I ruled that, in equity, ATCO Electric should not be required to pay further.
That does not detract from the fact that Carroll obtained the judgment in the first place.
11 Accordingly, I find that ATCO Electric is not entitled to double costs from the date of the second offer … 3.
Demand for Apology in Defamation Actions In Vaquero Energy Ltd. v.
Weir, 2004 ABQB 166, 2004 CarswellAlta 389, 352 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 254, the plaintiff successfully sued the defendant for defamation.
The plaintiff had served the defendant with a Rule 170 offer of settlement which required the defendant to pay $25,000 and to acknowledge responsibility for the defamatory remarks.
The issue was whether the demand for an acknowledgment of responsibility for the defamatory remarks fit within Rule 170.
Kent J. held that it did.
At p.
400, her Ladyship said: The defendant in this case says that because the court has no ability to order an apology, the plaintiff cannot demand it.
I disagree.
In a defamation action, a finding that what was said or printed was defamatory is often as important as the amount of a money judgment.
That finding is equivalent to a pre-trial apology.
A pre-judgment apology would serve the purpose of Rule 170, namely to encourage settlement.
Accordingly, an offer of judgment in a defamation action that includes a demand for an apology or acknowledgment falls within the scope of Rule 170.
When the Rule Results in Over Indemnification in Costs In Shillingford v.
Dalbridge Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 28, 2000 CarswellAlta 48, 268 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 361, Perras, J. held that costs calculated pursuant to Rule 174 should be awarded even if they result in a party receiving an over indemnification for his or her actual legal costs.
At p.

369, His Lordship said: It is my view, considering the above, that party/party costs where there has been a formal offer of settlement under the Rules of Court should be taxed based on the tariff amounts as set under Schedule C and as outlined in Rule 174, notwithstanding that [an] over indemnification may occur.
This would promote settlement by punishing those who refuse reasonable offers.
Furthermore, it would provide an even playing field irrespective of the actual cost of the lawyer, or the fact that a party is represented through legal aid or self represented. … In Jama v.
Bobolo, 2002 ABQB 216, 2002 CarswellAlta 435, 311 A.R.
362, 2 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 186, Clark J., at p.

191, said that: “Despite the possibility that over-indemnification may occur, it may indeed be appropriate to award double costs.” His Lordship implied that if the application of the provisions of Rule 174(2) would normally result in an award of double costs, the onus to show why that award should not exceed indemnification would fall on the party paying the costs.
He said, at pp.

191-192: Thus, the rule appears to be that if a party wants to continue to advance its claim, following an offer of settlement, it does so at its peril. … As there are no special reasons that would dictate in favour of restricting costs to indemnification in the present case, double costs are appropriate.
Reason for R.
4.29 People sometimes ask why a plaintiff who equals or beats her own offer gets higher costs.
There are two reasons.
First, unless a plaintiff's costs are going to be increased, there is no incentive whatever for the defendant to pay any attention to any plaintiff's offer to settle.
A plaintiff who recovers anything significant at trial will get single costs even without any offer.
Second, Rule 174 treats the plaintiff and the defendant similarily.
A defendant who equals or beats his own offer in effect gets double costs: (a) the defendant is awarded costs in his favour.
And (b) the plaintiff gets no costs despite her substantial recovery, though normally she would get full single costs.
A plaintiff who had neither made nor received any offer almost invariably gets full party-party costs of the suit, even if her pleadings claimed too much.
A party who sued for exactly what she is entitled and did not inflate her claim should not be penalized.
Jones v.
Trans America Life Insurance Co. of Canada (1996), 39 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 1 (C.A.), at 5, per curiam.
Purpose of R.
4.29(4)(a) In 864503 Alberta Inc. v.
Genco Place Properties Ltd., 2019 ABCA 248, 2019 CarswellAlta 1161, the Court said: … The purpose of rule 4.29(4)(a) is to avoid the doubling of indemnity or lump sum costs following a formal offer.
It does not have the effect of rendering a formal offer following an award of lump sum costs to be of no effect in respect of subsequent costs.
When Over-indemnification may constitute a “special circumstance” under R.
4.29(4)(e) In Mostafa Altalibi Professional Corporation v.
Lorne S.

Kamelchuk Professional Corporation, 2022 ABCA 364, 2022 CarswellAlta 3300, the Court discussed when over-indemnification might constitute a “special circumstance”: [34] In some circumstances, the possibility of significant over-indemnification may constitute a special circumstance to not award double costs.

For example, where solicitor and own client costs are awarded, this Court has stated that the doubling of such costs may constitute a special circumstance under r 4.29(4)(e): Boje v Boje (Estate of), 2005 ABCA 73 at para 39.
However, this Court also stated that the double costs regime may in some circumstances even apply to awards of solicitor and own client costs: Boje at para 39.

[35] The purpose of the double costs regime in the Alberta Rules of Court is to encourage settlement and to ensure that a party which “gambles and loses” on an appeal accepts greater consequences for doing so: H2S at para 18.
[36] In this case, no evidence has been provided that a double costs award would result in over-indemnification.
Absent such evidence, there is no basis to depart from the standard application of the double costs regime in the Alberta Rules of Court.
The respondents are seeking party-party costs, not solicitor and own client costs.
Therefore, the considerations identified in Boje do not apply here.
Double costs awards will be greater than standard costs awards by their very nature.
The mere possibility of over-indemnification is not a special circumstance within the meaning of r 4.29(4)(e).
Compare Offer to Judgment One should compare the offer to the judgment, but an issue arises concerning whether or not to include costs in the comparison.
In McAteer v.
Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 2003 CarswellAlta 654, 340 A.R.
1, 21 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 115, Rooke J. considered the question of determining whether an offer exceeded the judgment awarded.
At pp.
135-137, his Lordship said: There are two lines of authority that guide this comparison.
One method of calculating the value of an offer in relation to the judgment is discussed in Steve's Contracting Ltd. v.
Williams et al.
318 (Q.B.) (Andrekson, J.).
The court in that case acknowledged that there is very little Alberta case law that discusses this issue.
Accordingly, Andrekson, J., began his analysis with a review of the rule in Ontario that emanated from the decision in Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. v.
Cassina (1992), 15 C.P.C.
Gen Div.—Rosenburg, J.).
At p.
266 of that decision, the court found that: …the proper test is to look at the offer compared to the amount recovered plus interest and costs up to the date of the offer.
The court in Steve's Contracting looked at a number of decisions of the Alberta Court of Appeal in order to assess whether the same rule was applicable in Alberta.
It noted that in Ness v.
Leveridge (1995), 174 A.R.
L.R.
411 (Alta.
L.R.), the Court of Appeal stated, at para.
13 “The two ‘judgments’ must refer to amounts calculated in the same manner.” Cognizant of this requirement, the court, thus, compared the offer at para.

19 of Steve's: The plaintiff's offer … plus prejudgment interest to and including the date of the service of the offer, plus taxable party/party costs (including reasonable disbursements) for steps taken in all three actions up to and including the date of service of the offer is equal to or greater than the judgment amount … plus prejudgment interest to and including the date of service of the offer, plus taxable party/party costs (including reasonable disbursements) for steps taken in all 3 actions up to and including the date of service of the offer.
This formula has also been adopted by this court in Hillside Investments Ltd. v.
Boychuk, [2002] A.J.
No.
Uned.
231 (Q.B.—Marshall, J.) and Greep v.
Josephson et al.
326 (Q.B.) (Romaine, J.).
[59] The other line of authority suggests that costs should not be considered when comparing an offer to the judgment amount.
The Alberta Court of Appeal dealt with this issue in Pugsley v.
Wong et al., [2001] A.J.
No.
Uned.
At para.

4 the court, without citing any authority, in a very brief Memorandum of Judgment discussed the formula to be used in effecting a comparison: The reported cases on how to calculate whether the plaintiff has bettered an unaccepted offer usually compare damages and interest, not costs.
The reason for both things doubtless is rule 169(2), which allows a plaintiff, who accepts the defendant's offer, at once to tax her costs to that point.
Therefore, we conclude that we should not look at costs, and that the plaintiff plainly did not better the offer.
However, this comment in Pugsley appears to be obiter dicta.
Moreover, that case involved a situation where including the costs in the comparison would not have effected the result.
This fact was acknowledged by the court, at para.

6, where it stated “In case we are wrong, it probably would make very little difference here.” Additionally, the case deals with an offer by the defendant under the Rules which, as noted, allows the plaintiff to tax costs.
This is distinguishable from the case here, where the Offer was a Calderbank offer extended by the plaintiff which specifically included costs in its terms.
Finally, there is no suggestion that the Court of Appeal considered or even less so, intended, to reverse Ness.
In the result, I do not believe that I am bound by the obiter statement in Pugsley.
Rather, I find that the Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ness and cases to that effect are a better statement of the law in the context of the case at bar.
Examined from a principled point of view, I am of the view that the best approach is not to adopt a strict formula that will be used in all cases regardless of the terms of the offer.
There may be situations in which the comparison of costs is of little assistance.
One example would appear to be Pugsley.
In order to make a correct comparison, the total value of the offer must be considered in relation to the total value of the judgment as at the date of the offer.
In other words, it is inappropriate to exclude significant variables that may differ considerably.
In this case the judgment included an award of solicitor/client costs to Mason from the commencement of the Mason and Originating Notice Actions.
This amount differs considerably from the party/party costs that were included in the Offer.
It is therefore imperative that costs be included in the comparison in the present case.
In Alberta Wheat Pool v.
Fieldberg, 2001 ABQB 669, 2001 CarswellAlta 1007, 296 A.R.
161, the plaintiff offered to settle its claim by discontinuing its action if the defendant discontinued its three counterclaims, all without costs.

The defendant rejected the offer, and at trial, the plaintiff was awarded judgment in the amount of $41,770, two of the counterclaims were dismissed, and the third counterclaim resulted in the defendant (plaintiff by counterclaim) being awarded judgment in the amount of $611.36.
In deciding that the plaintiff was entitled to double costs because it had recovered judgment in excess of its offer, Lee J., at p.

166, said: …[T]he Offer that was made by Alberta Wheat Pool to settle this matter has a clear intent which was that both parties would walk away from their respective actions without either party receiving any costs.
My judgment was a substantive judgment of $41,770.00 in favour of the Plaintiff Alberta Wheat Pool, and essentially a nominal judgment of $611.36 on one of Mr.
Fieldberg's three Counterclaims, the other two Counterclaims being dismissed in their entirety.

Surely the Court should look at the overall intention of the Offer, and determine if based on that overall intention the Plaintiff was successful enough to earn double costs as part of a broad and liberal interpretation of Rule 174(2).
If Mr.
Fieldberg had accepted the Alberta Wheat Pool's Offer, he would have walked away owing nothing to the Alberta Wheat Pool.
It is clear that the Plaintiff has beaten its Offer in that Mr.
Fieldberg now owes them a net judgment of slightly over $41,000.00.

Given that the intention of the settlement provisions of the Alberta Rules of Court are to reduce the costs of litigation and encourage the resolution of lawsuits early, it is arguable that the Court should award double costs to the Plaintiff on both the claim and the Counterclaim for all steps taken after July 30, 1998.
However, given the possible confusion here arising out of the nature of the Offer of Settlement, I will award only double costs to the Plaintiff in its action against Mr.
Fieldberg in which it was clearly successful.
In Whitford v.
Agrium Inc., 2007 ABCA 109, 2007 CarswellAlta 445, the plaintiff made a formal offer to the defendant which was inclusive of costs and interest.
The offer was not accepted, and a judgment was awarded after trial.

The Court held that in determining whether the judgment obtained was more favourable to the plaintiff than the offer made, one must look at the costs and interest at the time of the offer, not at the time of judgment.
Slatter, J.A. said: 2 The plaintiff commenced a wrongful dismissal action against the defendant, and on September 9th, 2004 made a formal offer of $94,000.00, inclusive of costs and interest.
At trial in March of 2006 the plaintiff was awarded $81,834.78.
If costs and interest accrued to the date of the offer were added to the damage award, the judgment was less favourable than the offer.
However, if costs and interest accrued to the date of the judgment were added to the damage award, then the eventual result was more favourable than the offer.
The trial judge compared the offer to the judgment as if costs and interest to the date of judgment were included, and awarded double costs.
The question on this appeal is therefore how one calculates the amount of a judgment for the purpose of comparing it to an offer.
3 As a general rule, for the purposes of calculating costs, a judgment should be valued as if it included interest and costs up to the date of the offer only, not up to the date of trial.
The plaintiff's offer can only be “more favourable than” the judgment if the defendant would, on the date of offer, have been better off to accept the offer than suffer the eventual judgment.

It is inconsistent with the objectives of the Rules on formal offers to say that a plaintiff or a defendant can, by running up costs between the date of the offer and the trial, achieve a more favourable result.
When the offer is inclusive of costs, the proper approach is to add costs (including disbursements) and interest to the date of the offer, as set out in Steve's Contracting Ltd. v.
Williams (1997), 214 A.R.
318, Hillside Investments Ltd. v.
Boychuk, [2002] A.J.
No.
33, 2002 ABQB 26 at para.
6; McAteer v.
Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 21 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 116, at para.
60; and Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. v.
Cassina (1992), 15 C.P.C.
Gen.
Div.).

How the offeror came up with the amount of a lump sum offer, and what sub-components of the lump sum the offeror subjectively thought the offer contained, are not relevant to the assessment of whether the offer is “more favourable”.

In the end, the comparison is between the total amount of the offer, on the one hand, and on the other, the principal amount recovered on all heads of damage plus pre-judgment interest and costs (including disbursements) to the date of the offer.
4 The purpose of the rules is to encourage early reasonable settlements, thereby avoiding the costs and delay inherent in litigation.

To interpret the rules so as to allow costs and interest to be calculated right up to the date of judgment runs counter to those objectives because: a) it creates an incentive for the offeror to run up costs after the offer is made. b) at the early stages of litigation, where the required interlocutory steps and length of trial are uncertain and unpredictable, it would be difficult for the offeror to calculate, and the offeree to evaluate, an offer.

This is contrary to the policy of encouraging early settlement. c) it requires the offeree to pay a settlement premium or penalty equal to the costs of a trial, where the purpose of the rule is to avoid that trial and those very costs. d) a different rule would apply to offers inclusive of costs, compared to offers made “plus costs to be taxed”.

It is not suggested that a “plus costs” offer is properly compared to a judgment plus costs to the date of trial. … 7 In 2003, Rule 174(1)(b) relating to defendants offers was changed so that it also read “more favourable than”.
The wording “more favourable than” calls for a functional comparison of the judgment with the offer.
8 In this case the plaintiff's offer was clearly not more favourable than the judgment achieved.
One of the purposes of offers is to end litigation, thereby stopping the accrual of costs by both parties.
The offer by the plaintiff to accept $94,000 turned out to be more than what the defendant would have been liable to pay as of the date of the offer, and the defendant was entitled to reject it.

The plaintiff's offer turned out to be too high, and it cannot become “more favourable” simply because the plaintiff thereafter incurred more costs that a lower offer might well have avoided: Steve's Contracting at para.
9; Jones v.
Trans America Life Insurance Co. of Canada (1996), 39 Alta.
L.R.

Being Close Is Not Enough The Appellant urges, as one of the reasons why he should be awarded costs of the appeal, that the amount he recovered is very close to the amount paid in, and that the damages were low.
Therefore, he says, the Court should exercise a discretion not to apply the rule.
In my opinion, however, those factors, of themselves, would not entitle the Appellant to escape the effects of rule 174.
Rahmath v.
Louisiana Land & Exploration Co.
The Court of Appeal also stated: … the present R.
174 is designed to remove flexibility, absent truly “special reason”.
It appears to us that a near miss, or a payment into court only six days before trial, does not present such “special reason”.
Brown Estate v.
Young (1990), 73 Alta.
L.R.
In Patterson v.
Hryciuk, 2005 ABQB 136, 2005 CarswellAlta 309, 45 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 240, a plaintiff was granted judgment for $48,967.59 in a medical malpractice action.

She then sought costs “in excess of those prescribed under Column 2 of Schedule C”, claiming that “the Defendant refused to accept a Formal Offer to Settle served on him prior to trial which was ‘close enough’ to the judgment.” The judgment awarded was $1,032.41 less than the offer made by the Plaintiff.
Macklin J. declined to grant increased costs.
His Lordship said, at pp.
248-249: Rule 601(1) of the Alberta Rules sets out the factors which the court may consider when exercising its discretion in awarding costs.
They include the result in a proceeding and a number of other factors, none of which specifically include offers made by the parties to settle the matter prior to trial.
They do specify that the court may “consider any other matter relevant to the question of costs”.

There is also nothing in the compromise rules (Part 12, Rules 165 to 174) which would suggest that the court has discretion to take into account offers that do not meet the requirements set out therein for an award of additional costs.
They only speak in terms of offers that meet or beat the trial result.
Without an express provision allowing the court to consider inadequate but “close” offers, I do not feel it proper to consider them in determining the appropriate level of costs.
Rule 174 provides specific consequences where the Defendant refuses an offer and the judgment at trial is greater than the amount of the offer.
It does not allow consideration of the offer if it was close to or within a certain percentage of the award.
Where the rules are specific as to their effect, it is not appropriate to rely on a general provision to confer a benefit otherwise not earned.

Without any specific allowance for it, the court would be required in each case to assess the offer in light of the final result and demarcate a line over or under which the offer should be considered close enough to warrant cost consequences.

In terms of procedure, it is my view that unless there is a specific rule allowing a court to consider it, it is inappropriate for one party to hold up a compromise offer made by the other party and argue that the offeror should be somehow punished in costs for its inadequate offer.
Only offers that meet the requirements of the compromise rules, thereby allowing the court to consider them in its award of costs, should be brought to the attention of the court after judgment.

Unless and until there is a rule allowing the court to consider all offers made in writing (as in the other jurisdictions referred to above), those offers should be considered as having been made without prejudice and privileged for all purposes.
That is, they are irrelevant to the costs determination and should remain confidential as between the parties.

Further, and in any event, while the Defendant's offer may be seen as an unreasonable position given the outcome at trial, it is also a position that can easily be rationalized by a belief that there was no liability on the part of the defendant.
This is not a situation where the only issue was quantum and the defendant refused to consider payment of any amount notwithstanding its liability.
A defendant is entitled to defend an action and is entitled to maintain a defence on both liability and quantum.

Unless he refuses an offer that satisfies the requirements of the compromise rules and there is no other rule specifically allowing the court to consider the offer, the defendant should not be penalized by any increased award of costs.
In short, the Plaintiff is not entitled to any increase in its costs for serving an offer close to the judgment amount.
In Alberta, there is no single point for a missed field goal.

Onus Lies on Party Relying on the Rule In Alberta, the law as to who has the onus under Rule 174 to prove that a judgement obtained after trial was equal to or greater than his offer under Rule 170 is correctly set out in Stevenson & Côté's Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2000 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1999).
At page 134 the authors state: “The party relaying [sic] on the Rule has the onus of proving that he did better at trial than the offer”.
Madge v.
Meyer (2000), 77 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 391 (Q.B.) at 397, per Brooker, J.
Offer Must Satisfy High Degree of Certainty In Millott Estate v.
Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R.
307, 9 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 292, the plaintiff sought double costs under Rule 174(2) on the grounds that the plaintiff obtained at trial a judgment in excess of the offer the plaintiff had made to settle the action.

Fraser, J. in refusing the application noted that “[i]n the offer in question, the plaintiffs purported to reserve leave to seek advice and rulings from a Court of Queen's Bench Justice ‘as they in their sole unfettered discretion may determine’ on any and all issues concerning costs” (p.
Fraser J. said, at p.
314: The defendants also cite Laframboise v.
Billett (1991), 81 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 285 (Q.B.); rev'd on other grounds (1992), 5 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 394 (C.A.), in which MacLean, J.
(as he then was), stated (at para.
3): The consequences of the Rules as to costs contained in Part 12 of the Rules of Court are punitive, and therefore demand a very high degree of certainty and exactness.

The defendant's offer of settlement does not satisfy that high degree of certainty and exactness, and he is therefore not entitled to the benefit of those Rules and his application in that regard is dismissed.
Laframboise has been cited with approval in subsequent decisions, including Madge v.
Meyer et al.
L.R.
(2d) 285 (Q.B.), at para.
10 [Alta.
L.R.], and Garand v.
Mutual of Omaha Insurance Co. et al.
With respect, I adopt the principle underlying Laframboise, and find that service of the May 17 offer to settle did not, in the circumstances, require the doubling of fees.
Results of Mini-trial Are Irrelevant In Purich v.
Purich (1999), 248 A.R.
145 (Q.B.), the defendant in a support and matrimonial property action alleged that the plaintiff had not done as well at trial as had been earlier offered to her.
In support of that submission, the defendant referred to discussions which occurred in the mini-trial.
Veit J. held that mini-trials should not be considered when determining the issue of costs.
At pp.
147-49: The outcome of a mini-trial should not, without more, be taken into account in determining what costs should be paid at the conclusion of a trial. . . . . .
Settlement negotiations are, generally, privileged.

The privilege supports the under lying policy that fair settlements are a worthwhile objective and that parties should feel free to make concessions for the purposes of settlement which should not come back to haunt them if no settlement is, in fact, reached.
The Rules create a statutory interference with the privilege in order to give punch to certain, defined, types of offers of settlement.
The common law establishes that a party can put the party opposite on notice that if an offer of settlement is not accepted, that party intends to ask for costs.
Without such glosses of the privilege, no reference at all could be made to settlement negotiations at the costs hearing because those negotiations are privileged.
A mini-trial is just another form of settlement negotiations.

Without some legislated term or some understanding between the parties that the mini-trial will be referred to at the costs hearing, it is improper for the court to be advised of the results of a mini-trial.

Costs' Effect on Judgment Not a “Special Reason” In a defendant's application for double costs, the successful plaintiff submitted that these ought not to be awarded because this would effectively take from her the judgment granted to her at trial.
The court held that such a submission was irrelevant.

In the absence of exceptional circumstances, a court should not hesitate to award appropriate costs even if the results of the costs award would be to deprive a litigant of the financial benefit of the substantive litigation.
In this case, Ms.
Bates claims that if the court were to award costs to Mr.
Purich on the basis he proposes, the costs award would be so high that it would effectively deprive Ms.
Bates of the benefit of her judgment.
Ms.
Bates' argument is irrelevant.
The potential award of costs is meant to promote reasonable settlements.
If, indeed, there were a case where the costs were so high as to be equivalent to, or even higher than, the substantive amount in question, there should be an even greater impetus to be reasonable.
The court must make a costs determination on the basis of the principles that apply to such determinations.

The fact that a proper costs determination will deprive a litigant of the fruits of the litigation only proves that in that particular case, the litigation was pointless; for policy reasons, the unreasonable litigant should not profit in the slightest from unnecessary litigation.

Delay in an Action
Application to deal with delay

paragraphs.text: (1) If delay occurs in an action, on application the Court may (a) dismiss all or any part of a claim if the Court determines that the delay has resulted in significant prejudice to a party, or (b) make a procedural order or any other order provided for by these rules. (2) Where, in determining an application under this rule, the Court finds that the delay in an action is inordinate and inexcusable, that delay is presumed to have resulted in significant prejudice to the party that brought the application. (3) In determining whether to dismiss all or any part of a claim under this rule, or whether the delay is inordinate or inexcusable, the Court must consider whether the party that brought the application participated in or contributed to the delay.
